result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_kirchhoff_index()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the Kirchhoff index (total resistance) of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L29948-L30029){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Kirchhoff index](/assets/graphs/get-kirchhoff-index.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node graph labeled with the resistance distance across each edge: 1 on the two tail edges, but 0.75 on the four cycle edges (accent), where a second route runs in parallel. Summing resistance over all 15 pairs gives the Kirchhoff index 21.0." width="100%"} The Kirchhoff index is the sum of all pairwise resistance distances: `Kf(G) = Σᵢ<ⱼ Ω(i,j)` It can also be computed from the Laplacian eigenvalues: `Kf(G) = n × Σₖ (1/λₖ)` where `λₖ` are the non-zero eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Kirchhoff index. Returns `0.0` for single-node graphs. Returns infinity for disconnected graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Kirchhoff index $Kf(G) = \sum_{i < j} \Omega(i, j)$ (Klein and Randić, 1993) is the electrical analogue of the Wiener index, using effective resistance in place of shortest-path distance. A striking spectral identity ties it to the Laplacian directly: $Kf(G) = n \sum_{k \ge 2} \tfrac{1}{\lambda_k}$, summing reciprocals of the non-zero Laplacian eigenvalues, which makes small $\lambda_2$ (poor expansion) inflate $Kf$ and sharp expander graphs bring it down. Complete graphs saturate the lower bound $Kf \ge n - 1$; disconnected graphs give $+\infty$ because some resistances diverge. Cost is $O(n^3)$ via full Laplacian eigendecomposition, and only undirected inputs make sense because the electrical analogue requires reversibility. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path graph's Kirchhoff index grows with roughly the cube of its size, since resistance distances accumulate over many series connections: ::: {#0c8d7f5b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph() path.add_path_graph(4) # Returns 10.0 path.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 9.999999999999998 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph is the most efficiently connected case, so its Kirchhoff index is as low as possible: exactly `n - 1`: ::: {#72fc2d3f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} complete = ec.Graph() complete.add_full_graph(4) # Returns 3.0 complete.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3.0 ``` ::: ::: A disconnected graph has infinite resistance between components that can't reach each other, so the Kirchhoff index diverges: ::: {#1fe05595 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") # No edge between A and B # Returns inf g.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` inf ``` ::: :::
